 Vs.

full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury J: This criminal appeal, at the instance of the convict-appellant, is directed against the judgment and order dated 16-11-2008 passed by the learned Special Judge, Court No.9, Dhaka in Special Case No. 26 of 2008 arising out of Metro Special Case No. 139 of 2008 corresponding to Shah bag Police Station Case No. 27 dated 14-5-2008. By the impugned judgment and order, the learned Special Judge convicted the appellant under section 409 of the Penal Code, 1860 read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced him there under to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 5(five) years and to pay a fine of Taka 21,00,000 in. default, to suffer rigorous imprisonment for a further period of I ( one) year in absentia. 

 The accused-appellant ATM Nazimullah Chowdhury had been the Ambassador of Bangladesh to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) from March, 2006 to 30th June, 2008 on contractual basis. During his incumbency as Ambassador of Bangladesh to the UAE, certain allegations of corruption were leveled against him. As such, the informant Abdullah-al-Zahid (PW 1) was sent to the UAE to hold an inquiry into the allegations and accordingly he held a detailed inquiry therein to as per the order dated 16-3-2008 passed by the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) and found the same prima facie true. One of the allegations was that the accused-appellant hired a house at Mangrove village in the suburban area of Abu Dhabi at a distance of about 22 kilometres from the Bangladesh Chancery Building at an annual rental of 2,40,000 Dirhams from September, 2006 in preference to the earmarked rented residence of the Bangladesh Ambassador to the UAE near the Bangladesh Embassy at an amount of 2,10,000 Dirhams and because of shifting and other incidental expenses, the accused- appellant caused pecuniary loss of 72,000 Dirhams to the public exchequer. The second allegation was that he misappropriated the monthly salaries of the two alleged gardeners of the Embassy, namely, Jewel Miah and Selim Parvez to the tune of 34,150 Dirhams. Besides, he also misappropriated money on different heads by making payment of gas bill of his residence and some household articles purchased for his residence from a shopping mall, namely, Carrefour in Abu Dhabi purporting to show that those were used at the Embassy Office. Moreover, he spent 55 Dirhams from the public exchequer for binding of some personal books. In all, the accused-appellant misappropriated a sum of Taka 20,02,299 in Bangladesh currency from the public exchequer thus causing wrongful gain to himself and wrongful loss to the Government. After completion of the inquiry, the PW 1 Abdullah-al-Zahid lodged a formal ejahar with the Police Station concerned. After lodgment of the ejahar, the case was endorsed to him for investigation. Having taken up investigation of the case, he visited the place of occurrence, examined witnesses and recorded their statements under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He found the statements of witnesses which were recorded during inquiry similar to those recorded under section 161 of the Code. However, having found a prima facie case, he submitted the charge-sheet No. 336 dated 28-8-2008 against the accused-appellant under section 409 of the Penal Code, 1860 read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. 

 3. Because of the abscondence of the accused-appellant, the learned trial Judge charged him under section 409 of the Penal Code, 1860 read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 in absentia and ultimately the trial of the case had to be concluded as such. 

 10. In support of the above submissions, Mr. Fida M Kamal draws our attention to a number of decisions including the decisions in the cases of Abdul Bari Mollah vs State, 3 BLC474; Abul Khair vs State, 58 DLR 500; Abul Kalam Azad vs State, 48 DLR 294; Moslem Ali Mollah alias Moslem Mol/ah vs State, 48 DLR 427 and Mansur Ali vs State, 39 DLR 184. 

 14. Mr Abdur Rezzaque Khan, another learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that admittedly approval was accorded by the Foreign Ministry to hire a new residence for the Ambassador of Bangladesh in the UAE at Mangrove village at a distance of about 22 kilometres from the Chancery Building of Bangladesh Embassy and the expenditure incurred to the extent of 72,000 Dirhams were legally incurred and, as such, there is no question of incurring any criminal liability by the appellant on that count and since the appellant was found guilty on that count as well, the entire prosecution of the appellant was malafide. In order to buttress up this submission, Mr Abdur Rezzaque Khan relies on the decision in the case of Khondker Moshtaque Ahmed vs Bangladesh through the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs reported in 34 DLR (AD) 222. 

 17. Mr Harunur Rashid further contends that the provisions of section 222 and section 234 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are to be read conjointly and as the appellant was tried under the Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1958, the provisions of sub-section (lB) of section 6 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act will have primacy over those of the general law (Code of Criminal Procedure) and it is in sub-section (l B) of section 6 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act that a per- son accused of more offences than one punishable under the Act may be tried at one trial for all such offences and as sub-section (IB) is silent about the limitation of time with regard to the commission of any offence, the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 222 of the Code of Criminal Procedure will not come into play and this being the position, the learned trial Judge correctly framed charge against the appellant bearing the provisions of sub-section (IB) of section 6 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act in mind and in this view of the matter, it cannot be said that the learned trial Judge committed any illegality in trying the appellant under section 409 of the Penal Coderead with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. In support of this contention, Mr Harunur Rashid adverts to the decision in the case of Habibur Rahman Molla vs State reported in 61 DLR 1. 

 64. It is the submission of the learned Advocate Mr Abdur Rezzaque Khan that the entire prosecution of the accused- Ambassador is malafide in view of the approval accorded by the Foreign Ministry in respect of hiring of a new residential accommodation for the Bangladesh Ambassador in Abu Dhabi. The record shows that apart from this count, there are other counts on which the accused-Ambassador was arraigned. We do not think that merely because of prosecution of the accused-Ambassador on the score of incurring an additional expenditure of 72,000 Dirhams in respect of hiring of a new accommodation for the Bangladesh Ambassador in Abu Dhabi, the entire prosecution is malafide. The other heads of charge, as we see them, cannot be obliterated because of the alleged malafide prosecution of the accused-Ambassador as argued by Mr Abdur Rezzaque Khan. Furthermore, the decision relied on in the case of Khondker Moshtaque Ahmed vs Bangladesh through the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs reported in 34 DLR (AD) 222 by Mr Abdur Rezzaque Khan does not appear to have any applicability to the facts and circumstances of the instant case. Accordingly we feel constrained to hold that the above submission of Mr Abdur Rezzaque Khan is a shot in the dark. 

 66. What we are trying to drive at boils down to this: the provisions of section 222 and section 234 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are to be read conjointly and not in isolation. It goes without saying that the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 is a general adjective law whereas the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 is a special adjective law. In that view of the matter, the provisions of the special law will prevail over those of the general law. Sub-section (1B) of section 6 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act envisages that a person accused of more offences than one under this Act may be tried at one trial for all such offences. So it is seen that the limitation of one year as contained in the proviso to sub-section (2) of section 222 is not applicable for trial of a person accused of more offences than one under the' Criminal Law Amendment Act. In this respect, it seems that the learned Advocate for the Anti- Corruption Commission-respondent Mr Harunur Rashid has rightly relied on the decision in the case of Habibur Rahman Molla vs The State reported in 61 DLR 1. In that decision, it has been held that the period of one year is available in section 234 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; but it is absent in section 6(1B) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act and thereby section 6(1B) excludes the applicability of section 234 which relates to the period of commission of offences. So it is crystal clear that in respect of trial of offences punishable under section 409 of the Penal Code and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, the accused-Ambassador may be tried for all such offences irrespective of dates of commission of the same. 

 67. In this respect, the decisions in the cases of Abdul Bari Mollah vs State, 3 BLe 474; Abul Khair vs State, 58 DLR 500; Abul Kalam Azad vs State, 48 DLR 294; Moslem Ali Mollah alias Mos/em Mollah vs State, 48 DLR 427 and Mansur Ali vs State, 39 DLR 184 (supra) adverted to by Mr Fida M Kamal may be gone into. In those decisions, it has been clearly, categorically, unmistakably and ambiguously held that the vio- lation of the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 222 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in respect of framing of charge against an accused is not curable by section 537 of the said Code and, as such" the trials of those cases stood vitiated. But admittedly the provisions of sub-section (18) of section 6 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act were not brought to the notice of the Courts nor those were agitated by any party before the Courts. So necessarily there was no finding in place with regard to the primacy of the provisions of sub-section (18) of section 6 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act over those of section 222 and section 234 of the general law (Code of Criminal Procedure) in those decisions. Of course, at one stage, Mr Fida M Kamal has conceded to the primacy of the provisions of sub-section (18) of section 6 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act over those of section 222 and section 234 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Against this backdrop, the submission of Mr Fida M Kamal as to the alleged contravention of the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 222 of the Code of Criminal Procedure appears to be devoid of any substance. 

 80. In the case of Muhammad Sadiq Javeed vs State reported in 21 DLR (WP) 62, it has been held, inter alia, in paragraph 37: 

 82. Admittedly the learned trial Judge sentenced the accused-Ambassador in lump under section 409 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. This sentence in lump is a mere irregularity curable by section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Be that as it may, the learned trial Judge should have sentenced the accused-Ambassador under either of the sections of the two enactments keep-ing in view the legal position as spelt out in paragraph 37 of the decision reported in 21 DLR (WP) 62 (supra). 

 83. From the discussions made above and in the facts and circumstances of the case, we find the accused-Ambassador guilty under section 409 of the Penal Code, 1860 as well as under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The finding of conviction should be followed by an appropriate sentence under either of the sections of the two enactments. We think, the ends of justice will be sufficiently met if the accused-Ambassador is sentenced to 3(three) years rigorous imprisonment and to pay a fine of Taka 6,84,699, in default, to suffer rigorous imprisonment for a further period of 3(three) months under section 409 of the Penal Code. The impugned judgment and order stands modified accordingly.
